newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine central bank says peso still not normal.
newsitem.headline: Philippine central bank says peso still not normal.

text.p: The Philippine peso has still not found its true market level, despite settling between 28.50 and 29.00 to the dollar in recent days, a senior central bank official said on Tuesday.

"The exchange rate is still seeking its level in the market. (Although) the movement has been at a narrower range, the process of normalisation is not complete yet," central bank managing director Amando Tetangco told a lunch forum.

Sluggish trading at the Philippine Dealing System indicated that bankers and merchandise traders were not comfortable with the prevailing range, although he declined to say whether the rate should move higher or lower.
"There's still some degree of wait-and-see attitude," Tetangco said.
On Tuesday, the peso closed at 28.650 to the dollar in the official market, while the parallel market rate was hovering between 28.80 and 28.95.
The central bank had been intervening in the market, tempering the peso weakness at 28.85, traders said.
The uncertainties in the foreign exchange rate had made it difficult for the government to promote more investments, they said.
Board of Investments managing head Melito Salazar said in an earlier forum a weaker peso should attract more foreign investment into the country.
"But of course this is based on expectation that the inflation rate will not go up high," he told foreign journalists.
Domestic inflation is projected to creep up in the coming months following the oil price hike earlier this month and a possible new round of wage increases.
Salazar said it was too early to forecast a trend, although approved investment proposals in the first six months of the year had risen 152.7 percent to 199.53 billion pesos.
Tetangco said the central bank remained vigilant against a fresh speculative attack on the peso which led the central bank to declare a de facto devaluation on July 11.

It had since adopted several measures that tied the hands of speculators. These include temporarily suspending the sale of dollars through non-deliverable forwards, cutting banks' long dollar positions, increasing liquidity reserves of banks and reducing the allowable over-the-counter sales of dollars.
Tetangco declined to say whether more restrictions would be imposed in coming days, but said the Monetary Board was looking at the participation of banks' affiliates in the parallel market.
Foreign exchange corporations, which are usually affiliates of commercial banks, had been major players in the parallel market.
"We'll looking at it... We're looking at their activities since they are affiliates of banks," he said.

However, Tetangco said the central bank was not going to adopt recommendations made by a prominent local businessman who called on the central bank to compel exporters to surrender their export receipts and only allow importers with dollar requirements to buy dollars in the system.
"We're not thinking of going back to regulations," he added.
